attribution.note: Marcus's own bulleted assertion in his post. He states it in his own voice, not as a quote.

semantics.note: The claim is about present capability. 'Can produce copyright-infringing materials' keeps the scope; dropping 'fully' does not change the commitment.

contract.note: Reading 'infringe' as legal infringement, not just resemblance, is the ordinary informed reading. Pinning the capability to the quarter before publication is reasonable. Because the result depends on that legal threshold, interpretation matters.

evidence.note: NYT complaint (Dec 27, 2023) shows near-verbatim GPT-4 outputs, but whether they infringe is the plaintiff's contested allegation, not a finding.
OpenAI's own statement. It admits some regurgitation but disputes the legal claims. This is a company disclosure and contested evidence.
Chinese court found a GenAI image service's outputs infringed (Feb 2024). It involves a different provider, and the packet does not establish that those outputs fall in the target window.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows substantial reproduction by late-2023 systems. But it has no legal finding that outputs from the Oct–Dec 2023 window infringed: the NYT material is an allegation, OpenAI disputes it, and the timing of the Ultraman outputs is uncertain. No evidence shows the systems lacked the capability either. The packet does not settle the contract's legal threshold.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps the claim that OpenAI was not transparent about training data. 'Despite its name' is rhetoric and is rightly dropped.

contract.note: Reading transparency as identifying substantive sources, not every training example, is a fair ordinary reading. Using the quarter before publication is reasonable.

evidence.note: DALL-E 3 system card (Oct 3, 2023, read via an identified reproduction). It gives only broad categories, 'publicly available and licensed', and no source inventory. This is in-window documentation of what was disclosed.
GPT-4 report (Mar 2023) explicitly withholds dataset-construction details. It predates the window, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's in-window DALL-E 3 documentation gave only broad training-data categories and withheld the underlying sources. That meets the support condition. The earlier GPT-4 report's explicit withholding is consistent with this. Nothing in the packet shows a contemporary disclosure that substantially identified the sources.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: 'Will continue' is firm language, so this is a scored conditional forecast. The antecedent, 'often not at the request of the user', and the text/image scope are all kept. The normalised wording drops 'until', which is minor.

contract.note: The readings of provenance, invention versus deployment, 'often', and legal infringement are reasonable. But Marcus gave no deadline, reliability standard, frequency threshold, or jurisdiction, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: 2025 preprint shows generic prompts can produce copyrighted characters, which signals risk. It does not measure how often ordinary users infringe unintentionally, and it makes no legal finding.

Munich court press release (Nov 2025) found ChatGPT outputs infringed lyrics rights. This supports continuation in one case, but the judgment was not final and it does not address unrequested frequency or the antecedent.
2026 preprint on provenance gaps in code generation. It is a different domain and does not show that no qualifying text or image architecture exists.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and the early-resolution rule needs the antecedent plus recurring unintended legal infringement. The packet establishes neither: whether a qualifying provenance architecture exists is unknown, and the frequency of unrequested infringing outputs is unmeasured. The Munich ruling shows continued infringement in one case only. With the antecedent unknown, the forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: Only the factual clause, 'current systems don't', is normalised. The 'should' clause is normative and is correctly left out of scoring.

contract.note: In context Marcus is discussing attribution to underlying source materials, so a training-source manifest is the fair ordinary reading. The result does depend on excluding retrieval citations, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: MIT research synthesis written in December 2023 says provenance relationships were not supported in current foundation models. This fits the window and the reading.
Shows generative search engines gave in-line citations of retrieved pages. Those are not manifests of training sources, so this is a counterpoint only under a broader reading.

reviews.rationale: A synthesis written in December 2023 states that current foundation models did not preserve the provenance relationships needed for attribution. That supports the claim that mainstream systems gave no manifests of underlying sources. Bing Chat-style citations of retrieved pages do not meet the contract's definition of a manifest. No mainstream system in the packet provided one.
